extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers studying algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and collects definitions, theorems, and exercise-based criteria about cohomology of sheaves, degrees/lengths, Riemann–Roch, Serre duality, nef/ample/neumerical notions, and Hilbert polynomials for projective schemes and curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eilenberg–Zilber Theorem (cohomology of tensor product)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cohomology of the tensor product of two complexes over k is the tensor product of the cohomologies (Eilenberg–Zilber Theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a standard result to be used when comparing cohomologies of tensor products of complexes; no proof given here but referenced as known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cup product in Čech cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: The cup product in Čech cohomology can be defined in a simple way (see Liu, Exer. 2.17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as available construction; not needed for the immediate development but cited as an elegant description in the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of H0 and Hn on projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: H0(P^n, O(m)) should be interpreted as the homogeneous degree m polynomials in x0,...,xn (with A-coefficients). Hn(P^n, O(m)) should be interpreted as the homogeneous degree m Laurent polynomials in x0,...,xn, where in each monomial each xi appears with degree at most −1. (Remark 18.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation guides computations with Čech complexes and explains degree bookkeeping in cohomology computations on projective space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Čech complex for O(m) and degree-preserving maps
rubrics_metrics.description: The Čech complex for O(m) is the degree m part of a larger graded complex (displayed as (18.3.2.1)/(18.3.2.2)); the maps are natural inclusions or negatives thereof and preserve degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exactness can be checked multidegree-by-multidegree (monomial by monomial). The proof strategy splits into cases depending on the number of negative exponents in a monomial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre cohomological criterion for affineness (illustrated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 18.3.A: compute Hi(A^2_k \ {(0,0)}, O); in particular H1(A^2_k \ {(0,0)}, O) ≠ 0, so A^2_k \ {(0,0)} is not affine. (Cf. Serre’s cohomological criterion for affineness.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vanishing/nonvanishing of cohomology groups to detect (non)affineness via Serre's criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective k-scheme X and coherent sheaf F, χ(X, F) := Σ_{i=0}^{dim X} (−1)^i h^i(X, F). By Theorem 18.1.4 the hi(X,F) are finite so χ is finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euler characteristic behaves better than individual cohomology groups; it is additive in exact sequences and often easier to compute. Leading terms of dimensions of H0 on P^n show polynomial behavior in twists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity of Euler characteristic in exact sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If 0 → F → G → H → 0 is an exact sequence of coherent sheaves on a projective k-scheme X, then χ(X, G) = χ(X, F) + χ(X, H). More generally, for a finite exact complex Σ (−1)^i χ(X, Fi) = 0. (Exercise 18.4.A)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved via the long exact sequence in cohomology; used repeatedly to reduce computations of χ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Roch for line bundles on a regular projective curve
rubrics_metrics.description: χ(C, O_C(D)) = deg D + χ(C, O_C) for a divisor D on a regular projective curve C over a field k. (Essential Exercise 18.4.B)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction on the sum of absolute values of coefficients of D using the closed subscheme exact sequence and additivity of Euler characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of an invertible sheaf (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is an invertible sheaf on a regular projective curve C over k, define deg L := χ(C, L) − χ(C, O_C). (Exercise 18.4.C)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, for a nonzero rational section s of L with divisor D, deg L = deg D; compute degree by counting zeros and poles of any section not vanishing on a component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree behaves additively under tensor product
rubrics_metrics.description: If L and M are two line bundles on a regular projective curve C, then deg(L ⊗ M) = deg L + deg M. (Exercise 18.4.E)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: choose nonzero rational sections of L and M and count zeros/poles of their product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree under finite pushforward
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: C → C' is a degree d morphism of integral projective regular curves and L is an invertible sheaf on C', then deg_C π^*L = d · deg_{C'} L. (Exercise 18.4.F)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pullback of rational sections: zeros pull back to zeros and poles to poles; reduce to L = O(p) for a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic genus (definition and relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic genus pa(X) := 1 − χ(X, O_X). For integral projective curves over an algebraically closed field, h^0(X, O_X) = 1, so pa(X) = h^1(X, O_X). Riemann–Roch can be restated as h^0(C, L) − h^1(C, L) = deg L − pa(C) + 1. (18.4.2 and (18.4.2.1))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard form of Riemann–Roch used for curves; relates topological/geometric genus to cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank and degree of a coherent sheaf on a curve
rubrics_metrics.description: For an irreducible reduced curve C and coherent sheaf F, rank F is the rank at the generic point. If C is projective, define deg F = χ(C, F) − (rank F)·χ(C, O_C). (18.4.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank is additive in exact sequences (Exercise 18.4.H); degree is additive in exact sequences (Exercise 18.4.I) and for vector bundles equals degree of determinant bundle (Exercise 18.4.J).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ample line bundles on curves have positive degree
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is a projective curve and L is an ample line bundle on C, then deg L > 0. (Exercise 18.4.K)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: show it when L is very ample, then deduce for ample by taking powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for ampleness via induced morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is a base-point-free invertible sheaf on a proper variety X, inducing φ: X → P^n, then L is ample iff φ is finite. (Exercise 18.4.L)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If φ finite use Exercise 16.6.G; conversely if φ not finite find a contracted curve C and show L has degree 0 on C, contradicting ampleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: No rational sections of the universal plane conic (example constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no rational section to the projection π: C → P^5 of the universal plane conic; equivalently there are no nonzero rational functions X0,X1,X2 in the coefficients a_ij such that the conic equation a00 X0^2 + ... + a22 X2^2 = 0 holds with not all Xi = 0. (Exercise 18.4.P and discussion)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use degree/ intersection arguments (Exercises 18.4.O and 18.4.P) to derive a contradiction; illustrates arithmetic-topological interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of a module (definition) and composition series
rubrics_metrics.description: Length ℓ(M) is the length of the longest strictly increasing chain of submodules of M. A maximal such chain is a composition series; its subquotients are simple modules A/m. (18.4.7–18.4.8)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length generalizes vector space dimension; 0-module has length 0. Use composition series uniqueness (Jordan–Hölder type) as in Exercise 18.4.Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite length criterion for finitely generated modules over Noetherian local rings
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m,k) is Noetherian local and M finitely generated, then M has finite length iff m^n M = 0 for some n. (Exercise 18.4.R)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: finite length modules over such rings are built from finitely many copies of k = A/m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Roch for nonreduced curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 18.4.S: For a projective curve C (possibly nonreduced) and coherent sheaf F, χ(L ⊗ F) − χ(F) equals the sum over irreducible components C_i of deg(L|_{C_i^{red}}) times the length of F at the generic point η_i of C_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: reduce to scheme-theoretically supported on C^{red} using filtrations by powers of the ideal sheaf; write L as O(Σ n_j p_j) and use induction on number of points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical equivalence and Pic_τ (numerically trivial line bundles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define deg_C L = deg_C i^* L for i: C ↪ X; L is numerically trivial if deg_C L = 0 for all one-dimensional closed reduced subschemes C. Numerically trivial invertible sheaves form subgroup Pic_τ X; N1(X) := Pic X / Pic_τ X. The Picard number ρ(X) = rank N1(X). (18.4.9–18.4.10)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notions lead to Néron–Severi group and numerical invariants; finiteness (Theorem of the Base) is nontrivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nef (numerically effective) line bundles and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: An invertible sheaf L is nef if deg_C L ≥ 0 for all integral curves C in X. Nefness is a numerical property. (Definition 18.4.11)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: L nef iff deg_C L ≥ 0 for all integral curves C; pullbacks of nef are nef; nef on components equivalent to nef globally; nef elements form a semigroup in Pic X; ample implies nef; and L is nef iff some positive power is nef (Exercise 18.4.V).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nef cone and Q-line bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: For Q-line bundles, nef Q-line bundles form a closed cone in N1_Q(X), called the nef cone. Ample divisors form a cone whose interior equals the ample cone; for projective X the ample cone is the interior of the nef cone (Kleiman's criterion). (Exercises 18.4.W and discussion)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes convex-geometric viewpoint: nef/ample are detected by intersection with curves; boundaries correspond to contractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre duality (existence of dualizing sheaf and perfect pairing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 18.5.1: For a geometrically irreducible smooth projective k-variety X of dimension n there is an invertible sheaf ω_X such that hi(X, F) = h_{n−i}(X, ω_X ⊗ F^∨) for all finite rank locally free sheaves F, and a perfect pairing H^i(X,F) × H^{n−i}(X, ω_X ⊗ F^∨) → H^n(X, ω_X) ≅ k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ω_X is a dualizing sheaf; smoothness can be relaxed and the pairing arises from duality theory (to be connected to canonical bundle later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical sheaf equals determinant of cotangent bundle
rubrics_metrics.description: The invertible sheaf ω_X turns out to be the canonical sheaf (canonical bundle) K_X, defined as the determinant of the cotangent bundle Ω_{X/k}. (18.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies the abstract dualizing sheaf from duality theory with the concretely constructed bundle of top-degree algebraic differential forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre duality example on P^1
rubrics_metrics.description: For P^1, ω_{P^1} ≅ O(−2). There is a natural perfect pairing H^0(P^1, O(n)) × H^1(P^1, O(−2−n)) → k given by multiplication and reading the coefficient of x^{−1} y^{−1}. (18.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a concrete model for the abstract pairing in Serre duality using homogeneous (Laurent) polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of vector bundles on P^1 (Grothendieck's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 18.5.6: Any rank r vector bundle E on P^1_k splits as E ≅ ⊕_{i=1}^r O(a_i) for unique nondecreasing integers a_1 ≤ ... ≤ a_r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses cohomological arguments (Hom(O(m), E) computations, Serre vanishing/duality optionally). Horrocks' criterion is mentioned as a higher-dimensional generalization (splitting when middle cohomology of all twists vanishes). Exercises guide uniqueness and induction steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function and Hilbert polynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a coherent sheaf on a projective k-scheme X ⊂ P^n, define h_F(m) := h^0(X, F(m)). Theorem 18.6.1: χ(X, F(m)) is a polynomial in m of degree equal to dim Supp F; for m ≫ 0 higher cohomology vanishes and h^0(X, F(m)) equals this polynomial p_F(m). Definition 18.6.2: p_F(m) is the Hilbert polynomial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes eventual polynomiality of Hilbert functions; the degree of p_F gives geometric dimension information and leading coefficient relates to multiplicities/degree.
